common_name: Black Prince Echeveria (Near-Black Deep Purple Rosette Succulent)

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; Black Prince forms a tight rosette of near-black, deep purple leaves, among the darkest-colored echeveria hybrids available.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining, gritty cactus-and-succulent mix; deep, saturated color requires bright light, and the rosette fades toward green in low light. Black Prince, a hybrid derived from Echeveria affinis and E. shaviana parentage, forms a tight, symmetrical rosette of pointed, near-black, deep purple leaves, one of the darkest-colored echeveria hybrids commonly grown, providing dramatic contrast against paler succulents in a mixed container or rock garden. It sends up striking red-orange bell-shaped flowers on tall stalks in the growing season. Water only when the soil is fully dry, avoid wetting the leaves, and provide bright light to prevent the rosette from stretching and losing its tight, dark-colored form.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

common_name: Blue Tango Bromeliad (Pink Bract with Blue-Tipped Flower Spike)

planting.note: Grow in containers or protected shade in zone 10-11, or as a houseplant elsewhere; Blue Tango Aechmea has no frost tolerance. It bears a bold hot-pink bract topped by small blue-tipped flowers on a branched spike.

directions: Give bright, filtered light or partial shade; Aechmea bromeliads scorch in direct hot sun but need good light to flower and hold their best color. Blue Tango produces a dramatic, long-lasting hot-pink branched bract topped with small blue-tipped flowers that fade to pink as they age, held well above the broad, silver-banded, arching leaves in a classic urn-shaped rosette. Like other Aechmea it flowers only once per rosette, after which offsets, or pups, form at the base and can be separated and repotted once they reach about a third the size of the parent. Keep the central cup topped with water, and grow in a loose, fast-draining bromeliad or orchid mix rather than heavy garden soil.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Bromeliads for the home and landscape
